6-1 Balance of Payments  
**Balance of payments** \- the summary of a country’s transactions with other countries

Look at:

**Current account** (CA)

1) Balance of payments on goods and services (exports & imports)  
2) Factor income (R \+ W \+ I \+ P)  
   1) Income down → amt. Exports down → CA up because fewer outflow  
3) International transfers   
   1) **Transfer payment** \- any time money exchanges hands without a good, asset, or resource being provided in exchange  
   2) Often, **remittances** (when someone goes to another country to work and sends the money home)  
4) Does not create liabilities → don’t have to pay back interest or profits

**Capital & financial account** (C**FA**)  \- tracks assets

- If governments are lending/borrowing – official/public assets  
- If households/firms are lending/borrowing → private assets (whether in our country or not)  
- Creates liabilities → have to pay borrowing & interest back

Difference between asset itself & the dividends/profits from assets

- Interest & profit \= factor payments  
- Asset itself is part of CFA  
- Dividend/interest/profit part of CA

If only looking at goods, use merchandise trade balance

Circular flow assumes that CA \+ CFA \= 0

Surplus on CA must mean deficit in CFA & vise versa

When thinking about balance of payments → look @ ledgers

- Won’t usually have to write out on own

How do we model our balance of payments?

Exports \- imports → more money flowing into country on current account

- Aggregate demand go up → GDP up

If exports are higher than imports 

- AD down  
- GDP down

**Financial investment** \= National savings \+ capital inflow/outflow

Financial investment \= borrowers \+ savers

If have a deficit for capital inflow, would be capital outflow

**Capital inflows** \- money flowing into the country from foreign investors 

- Savings from foreign investors

**Capital outflows** \- money from country’s savers flowing out to different countries

Make assumptions to simplify

- Assume all assets are in form of loans (stock, bonds, mutual funds, etc.) so we can use market for loanable funds  
- Ignore effects of expected changes in **exchange rates** (**XR**)  
- Assume ease of access → ease of borrowing & lending to other countries

Tracking our country relative to another in MLF graphs  
![][image1]

Considerations:

- Politics  
- Pretend business cycles of each country do not play a role  
- Pretending ease of transaction between countries

6.2 Foreign Exchange  
If you want to buy g/s from another country (import) or invest in assets from that country (capital outflow) you demand their currency (and supply their currency)

If someone from another country wants to buy from the US or invest in assets from our country (capital inflow) they must supply their currency (and they demand our currency)

**XR (exchange rate)**  today: \$1 \= 1 euro

If changed to \$1=.8 euros, have to spend \$1.25 to get a full euro

- More dollars to buy the euro  
- Dollar divided by euro   
- Dollar has depreciated  
- Euro has appreciated

**Appreciated** \- currency bcomes more valuable in terms of other currencies

- Price of goods and services from other countries (imports) goes down

**Depreciation** \- currency becomes less valuable in terms of other currencies

- Prices of imports rise, so fewer imports from other countries

![][image2]

Considerations of Foreign Exchange

International business cycles → change in aggregate demand impacts foreign exchange \+ Foreign exchange impacts aggregate demand

- Changes in curves (price level, interest rate) will change balance of payments and therefore exchange rates  
- Will then impact aggregate demand 

Opposite impact on stabilization policies

- Ex. Interest rate start to go up bc of contractionary monetary policy. BUT THEN bc of capital flows, more ppl. From elsewhere Want to invest in the U.S. → opposite of what wanted

Protectionism \+ barriers to trade \+ capital flow

- No easy access 🙁  
- Looks easier on paper

Inflation \+ real XR

- **Purchasing power parity** \- between two countries’ currencies is the nominal exchange rate at which a given market basket would cost the same amount in two different countries   
- Compare nominal and real values  
  - Careful of inflation and classification of values when comparing countries

RealXR \= £/\$ \= (CPI US) / (CPI) UK

XR policy

- 2 types:  
- **Floating** \- what we’ve been doing the whole time; XRs determined by supply and demand of currency  
- **Fixed** \- when you try to control supply and demand of currency


  Pros of fixed XR

| pro | con |
| :---- | :---- |
| Not as exposed to international business cycles | Takes work to revalue and devalue currency |
| Try to control currency / foreign exchange rate | More gov. Intervention in economy |

  Revalue & devalue \= appreciate & depreciate

# Stabilization Policies in Focus 

## (5-1) Considerations of Fiscal Policy

Do we do demand or supply side → tendency to do demand side, but sometimes it has drawbacks like with stagflation

**Supply side** \- impacts producers

- Decrease business taxes  
- Decrease regulation on business  
- Increase subsidies

Must be careful because it impacts firms’ investments, which impacts aggregate demand

Demand side

- Raise GDP  
- Lower taxes  
- Increase transfers

Considerations of fiscal policy  
**Lags** \- the additional time something takes

- **Recognition lag** \- takes extra time to recognize the problem  
- **Decision lag** \- takes extra time to fix issues bc of a lack of decisions  
- **Implementation lag** \- takes time to implement decisions (ex.: Building a bridge)

**Human behavior** \- doesn’t always respond the expected way

- Ex.: stimulus checks

Fiscal policy not perfect because we may have to reverse the policy just made to account for 

Might want to change fiscal policy for other reasons besides than impacting business cycle

Savings of Government \= inflows \-  outflows  
Savings of Govermnet \= taxes \- (G \+ transfers)

**Expansionary fiscal policy** \- Taxes go down, Government spending goes up, Transfers go up

**Budget deficit** \- When outflows are greater than inflows

- AKA Negative budget balance  
- Have been running a budget deficit since the Clinton administration → debt bc they must borrow to cover funds  
  - Gov. borrows through bonds

**Contractionary Fiscal Policy** \- taxes up, government spending down, transfers down

**Budget surplus** \- positive budget balance

Considerations of national debt

- **Crowding out the market** \- if the gov. Is borrowing, it’s impacting the market for loanable funds → increases the demand of loanable funds curve  
  - Government taking loanable funds, meaning that households and firms can’t, also pushes interest rates (cost of borrowing) up

**Implicit liabilities** – assumption that the government is going to pay for certain things

Debt to GDP ratio \=  size of debt/GDP

Considerations with Monetary Policy  
**Lags** \- the additional time something takes

- **Recognition lag** \- takes extra time to recognize the problem  
- **Decision lag** \- takes extra time to fix issues bc of a lack of decisions  
- **Implementation lag** \- takes time to implement decisions (ex.: Building a bridge)

**Liquidity trap** \- when interest rates begin to approach 0% (zero bound)

- As this happens, traditional tools of monetary policy essentially become ineffective → this is why we switch from having limited to ample reserves

**Money neutrality** \- 

- in the short run, changes to the money supply can impact interest rates and GDP  
- In the long run, nothing real (accounting for inflation) changes  
  - Nominal changes → only real change is the inflation/APL up

If money supply changes by a certain percentage, the size of the change of the \$ supply will \= the size of the change of the money demanded \= size of the change of APL \= total change

If \$ supply goes up 20%, MD will go up 20%, APL will go up 20%

**Quantity theory of money** \- 

**V \= velocity of money** \- \# of times money is spent in a period of time

- Saving in cash \= low velocity  
- Spent dollars \= 

M x V \= nominal GDP \= P x Y

**M \= money supply**

**P \= price of things sold**

4-1 & 4-2 Financial Assets  
\-The major types of financial assets in the financial sector. Your notes should include a definition of each of the financial assets (loans, stocks, bonds) as well as notes on the difference between assets and liabilities.

**Financial sector** \- money is channeled between savers who invest their current savings or wealth into financial assets for borrowers who need \$ for spending

- Transforms money saved by savers into funds for borrowers who need \$ for spending

**Savings investment identity** \- invest savings (savers \= investors)

**Wealth** \= accumulated savings

Lender \- 

**Cash**

- Most familiar  
- Opportunity cost → no interest (doesn’t grow)  
- Can be the most convenient in some situations

**Interest rate** \- the price, calculated as a percentage of the amount borrowed, charged by lenders to borrowers for the use of their savings

Even holding \$ in checking acct. Has a trade off → can earn higher interest rate with \$ in other assets

Must weigh the convenience of holding cash over its opportunity cost

**Financial markets** \- where households invest their current savings and their accumulated savings, or wealth, by purchasing financial assets

**Commodities** \- things with intrinsic value

- Are used as money  
- Gold, silver, etc.   
- Challenges: 	  
  - People would get robbed  
  - Transportation

Transitioned to c**ommodity-backed money** → pieces of paper that were worth the commodity → trade commodities into bank in exchange for paper money  
Move off from gold standard to **fiat money**  
   
**Fiat money** \- not backed by a commodity 

- Valuable because the government says it’s money, and we believe it

**Wealth** \- value of a household’s accumulated savings

Money \- any asset that fulfills these three roles:

1) Medium of exchange  
2) Store of value \- retains value over time  
3) Unit of Account \- helps us make economic calculations and to compare prices

**Financial Asset** \- a nonphysical asset that entitles the buyer to future income from the seller

- Something we own  
- Ex.: a saver lends funds to a company, the loan is a financial asset sold by the company and purchased by the saver → loan entitles the saver to future income from the company

**Physical asset \-** tangible object that the owner has the right to use or dispose of as they wish

- Ex.: house, car, equipment, etc. 

**Liability** \- requirement to pay money in the future (including interest)

- Creating a loan \= creating a liability  
- Even though a loan is a financial asset from bank’s POV, it’s a liability from borrower’s POV

3 tasks of financial system

1) Reduce transaction costs  
   1) **Transaction costs** \- expenses of actually putting together & executing a deal  
   2) A bond market allows companies to borrow large sums of money without incurring large transaction costs  
2) Reducing Risk  
   1) **Financial risk** \- uncertainty about future outcomes that involve financial losses & gains  
   2) The desire of individuals to reduce their total risk by engaging in diversification is why we have stocks and a stock market  
3) Providing Liquidity  
   1) **Liquid assets** \- can be quickly converted into cash without much loss of value  
   2) **Illiquid assets** \- cannot be quickly converted into cash without much loss of value  
   3) Sale of stocks and bonds can resolve some liquidity issues by raising money for new projects  
   4) By taking deposits & lending them, banks let people own liquid assets while financing illiquid asset investments (ex.: businesses & homes)

**Liquidity \-** how easily something can be converted into cash

Types of financial assets:

1) **Loan** \- a lending agreement between an individual borrower & individual lender  
   1) Mostly in form of bank loans for car or house  
   2) Creates transaction costs associated with identifying qualified buyers

2) **Bonds** \- interest-bearing asset that represents a loan to a company or government  
   1) Can be thought of as an IOU  
   2) Financial asset from owner’s point of view & liability from issuer’s POV  
   3) Bond purchasers can get info on the bond issuer (ex.: credit history) from bond-rating industries  
   4) Easy to resell \- provide liquidity to bond purchasers  
   5) When interest rate in econ. Falls, preexisting bond prices usually rise  
3) **Stocks** \- a type of equity that represents ownership of that company  
   1) Share in the ownership of a company   
   2) **Equity** \- ownership in the value of an asset or business  
   3) Shareholders enjoy a higher rate of return over time in comparison to bonds  
   4) A bond is a promise, a stock is a hope  
   5) Higher return & higher risk 

Calculating Nominal Interest Rates  
**Nominal interest rate** \- interest rate actually paid for a loan, unadjusted for inflation

- Nominal interest rate \= real interest rate \+ inflation rate

**Real interest rate** \- the nominal interest rate adjusted for inflation

- Real interest rate \= nominal interest rate \- inflation rate  
- Takes opportunity cost of loaning funds & value of what can be purchased after an increase in prices into account

Bc interest rate on loan is determined before loan is made, actual rate of inflation over period of the loan will not be known

Expected real interest rate \= nominal interest rate \- expected inflation rate

Nominal interest rate \= expected real interest rate \+ expected inflation rate

If the actual inflation rate is higher than expected, borrowers gain at the expense of lenders

- Borrowers repay loans with funds that have a lower real value than had been expected

If the actual inflation rate is lower than expected, lenders will gain at the expense of borrowers

- Borrowers must repay their loans with funds that have a higher real value than had been expected

Nominal interest rates charged by lenders don’t go below zero, but real interest rates can be negative

Interest rates give us a measure of the price of money that is borrowed or saved

**Money supply (M)** \- the assets in the economy considered to be money that are circulating around the economy

**M1 \=**  

- currency in circulation → dollars and coins  
- Demand deposits → checkable bank deposits; money in our checking account  
- Savings accounts → short-term savings accounts \- liquid enough to be counted

**M2 \=** 

- All of M1  
- Near moneys (like short term CDS \+ money market funds)

**Near money** \- any asset that is not as liquid as the assets in M1, but they are pretty darn close

- Ex.: short term CDs, short term Money market funds

**Mo/Mb** \= **monetary base**:

- Currency in circulation  
- Bank reserves

Money supply impacts APL \+ interest rates

As technology advances, it impacts APL % Interest rates

Interest provides 2 purposes:

1) Compensate lender for lending services  
2) Account for inflation

Differentiate between long and short term interest

- i= nominal interest rate  
  - Short term  
- r=real interest rate  
  - Long term

Constantly thinking of spenders & savers; pov

- Lend money → true profit \= interest

Borrowers talk interest

Diversify portfolio for investing

We buy bond from gov. → bonds have inverse interest rate, meaning that when interest rates go up, bond prices go down

Money supply up, interest rate down depending on saver or borrower role  
When \$ supply goes down, interest rates go up

Savers

- Interest rate down, hold onto money rather than invest  
  - Opportunity cost of holding money goes down  
  - Lead to consumption going up  
- Interest rate up, opportunity cost of holding money goes up  
  - Choose to put into assets → cant use it to buy → C goes down

Borrowers

- Interest sensitive   
  - If interest rate go down, more people buy student loans, etc.  
  - More consumption up \+ I, \+AD  
- Interest rate up  
  - More expensive  
  - Firms might not invest in capital   
  - Consumption down

**Financial intermediaries** \- where money is channeled between savers and borrowers

- **Pensions**  
- **Mutual funds** \- work same as life insurance  
  - Asset, but a diversified portfolio of assets  
  - Contributing money into different assets → invested, we get a cut of the profits  
- **Life insurance** \- work same as mutual funds  
- **Banks** \- 

***IN EVENT OF BANK RUNS***

**Bank runs** \- starting to enter recession → a bunch of people go to withdraw money from checking & savings → when banks ran out of money (savings & checking is in loans to others), they would close, sometimes for good

**Monetary base** \- currency in circulation \+ bank reserves

**Reserves** \- when a bank holds money in its vault or its account at the Fed. → not part of Money Supply, but is part of monetary base

- **Reserve Ratio** → fraction of deposits held in reserves  
- **Excess Reserves** → the remaining reserves beyond the minimum amount set by the fed. 

If banks don’t have enough money in required reserves, They can contact other banks to see if they have excess reserves that they can borrow

- Banks must pay interest on money borrowed from other banks → interest follows the country’s prevailing interest rate  
  - **Federal Funds Rate** → policy banks follow to charge interest rate to other banks (AKA **Policy Rate**) → influenced but not directly controlled by the Fed.   
- Can borrow money from **federal reserve**  
  - **Discount rate** \- interest charged by Fed. to banks borrowing from Fed.   
    - Directly controlled by Fed. → set to be 1% higher than federal fund rate to incentivize going to smaller banks & using Fed as last resort

**Capital requirements** \- other assets that the bank must own

**FDIC \- Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation** \- The government will insure up to \$250,000 in deposits for every account owned in case of depression/recession and bank runs begin

**Money Multiplier (MM)**  \-  one dollar deposited into the banking system multiplies to more than one dollar circulating around the economy

- Indicates the maximum \# of dollars created in the banking system by each additional dollar added to the Monetary Base  
- The ratio of the money supply to the Monetary base  
- KNOWING THIS SEPARATES 4s from 5s  
- MM \= 1/Reserve Ratio  
- Based on an increase of excess reserves (more in excess reserves, more can be lent out)  
- Works same as **spending multiplier**

Graphing the liquidity of money

True cost of borrowing is interest

Balance between liquidity and wanting to put \$ into financial assets to gain interest

- As interest rates go down, opportunity cost of holding money goes up  
- As interest rates rise, opportunity costs of holding money goes down

**Shifters of \$ Supplied:**

* Set by Federal Reserve in an economy with limited resources

**Shifters of \$ Demanded:** 

* Changes in APL  
  * Higher aggregate prices → MD↑  
  * Lower aggregate prices → MD↓  
* Change in Real GDP (Y) driven by a change in spending → more consumption happening in the economy  
  * Increase in real GDP → MD↑  
  * Decrease in real GDP → MD↓  
* Changes in financial technology  
  * Advances in financial technology → MD↓  
* Changes in Financial Institutions  
  * Regulations that make it more attractive to keep money in banks → MD↓  
  * Political strife/dangerously unstable banking conditions → MD↑

4.6 Monetary Policy  
**Inflation targeting** \- occurs when central bank sets explicit target for the inflation rate and adjusts monetary policy in order to hit that target

Banks will conduct monetary policy in response to an inflationary or recessionary gap → works by shifting aggregate demand curve through effect on interest rate  
![][image8]  
![][image9]

**Expansionary monetary policy** increases aggregate demand 

- Decreases interest rates, which increases aggregate demand and therefore GDP

**Contractionary monetary policy** reduces agregate demand

- increases interest rates, which lowers aggregate demand and therefore GDP

**Overnight interbank lending rate** \- interest rate that banks charge other banks for overnight loans

- Policy rate of central bank is its target range for an interbank lending rate

**Federal funds rate** \- interest rate in the federal funds market, where banks make overnight loans to each other

**Limited reserves** \- reserves are scarce and relatively small changes in supply of reserves shifts the money supply curve and changes the interest rate

**Ample reserves** \- opposite of limited reserves, changes in supply does not significantly change interest rate

![][image10]

While central banks change the reserve requirement, they also affect interest rates increasing the percentage of their deposits that they lend, leading to supply more loans and increase the money supply (money multiplier)

If reserve ratio requirement is incresed, banks must reduce lending, leading to a fall in money supply, higher interest rates, and lower GDP

Monetary policy in Econ. With Limited Reserves   
**Discount rate** \- the interest rate the central bank charges on loans to banks

- Banks respond to a decrease in the discount rate by incresing their lending to increase money supply & reduce the interest rate in the economy  
- Opposite to an increase in discount rate

**Open market operations (OMOs)** \- include the purchase or sale of government debt (ex.: a bond) by a central bank

- Through these operations, the central bank controls the monetary base (bank reserves \+ currency in circulation) → influence money supply & interest rates in economy with limited reserces

Modern monetary policy tools  
**Zero bound** \- when the short-term interest rate has already been lowered to zero; economic stimuli requires central bank to use nontraditional policy

- Inability to lower the federal funds rate below zero

**Quantitative Easing** \- expansionary monetary policy that involves central banks purchasing longer-term government bonds and other financial assets

**Interest on Reserce Balances (IORB)** \- amt. Central bank pays in interest to banks for their balances held in reserve

- Interest on reserves \- the rate the central bank pays in interest to banks for holding reserves rather than holding other financial assets

Policy in an economy with ample reserves 

![][image11]

**Monetary policy** lags result from the time it takes to recognize a problem in the economy & the time it takes for a monetary policy action to take effect in the economy  
![][image12]

Limited v. Ample reserves (what they did to go from limited to ample reserves)

- **Stricter regulation** in the financial system  
- **Quantitative easing** → supplying bank reserves with a lot of liquidity  
  - Want reserves to be available to banks  
  - Open market operations on a large scale  
- **Reserve requirement** \= 0%  
  - Make money multiplier infinite  
- **Interest on reserve balances (IORB)** \- interest that banks get on reserves  
  - Incentivize banks to keep money in reserves by allowing interest on it (profit for banks)  
  - Usually only used when the reserve requirement \= 0%  
  - Sometimes just called interest on reserves (IOR)  
  - Directly controlled by the Fed → **an administered interest rate**

**IOR & discount rate** are both **administered interest rates**

Federal funds rate is only *influenced* by the Fed, not administered

**Policy rate** \- prevailing interest in economy

- The interest rate banks care most about is the Federal Funds rate (used in overnight borrowing & lending between banks)

Demand for Reserves \-

**National Income and Price Determination**

3.1 \- Income and expenditure  
Remember: Expenditure approach → Y \= C \+ I \+ G \+ (Ex. \- Im.)

Thinking of the economy as a closed economy for now → ignore government spending and Net Exports

Spending has to do with our disposable income

**Disposable income (Yd)** \- amt. Of income available for consumption and savings

- Yd \= inflows \- taxes  
  - Inflows \= income, transfer payments like social security  
- Yd \= C \+ S    (consumption \+ savings)

Savings \= investment & wealth

**Wealth** \- accumulated savings

**Autonomous consumption (a)** \- the idea that we will spend money even when our disposable income is zero

- Loans, credit cards, debt  
- Dipping into savings

**Marginal propensity to consume (MPC)** \= ∆C/∆Yd

- With an additional dollar, how much will be used to consume

**Marginal propensity to save (MPS)** \=  ∆S/∆Yd

- With an additional dollar, how much will be used to save

**Spending multiplier (M) \-** indicates the total rise in GDP that results from each additional \$1 of an initial rise in spending

- That additional dollar is the **autonomous change in aggregate spending (AAS)**  
  - **AAS** \-  the initial rise or fall in aggregate spending that is the cause – not the result— of a series of income spending \+ spending changes  
- One dollar of spending in one area of the economy multiplies to more than one dollar circulating around the economy  
- Bluey video

MPC \+ MPS \= 1

M \=  ∆GDP/ ∆AAS            M \= 1/1-MPC           M \= 1/MPS

3.2  \- aggregate demand  
Looking at the demand across the entire economy

- Graphed on the macroeconomy graph

GPL \= APL

Moving from point to point has a negative slope because…

- **Real balances or wealth effect** \- when aggregate price levels impact how much wealth we feel we have, which impacts how much we demand in aggregate  
- **Interest rate effect** \- when aggregate price levels impact interest rates, which impacts the aggregate demand/level of spending across the economy  
- **Exchange rate effect** \- when the aggregate price levels impact the value of our currency against another’s, which will impact the price of our goods relative to another country’s and financial investments between countries  
- ALL ARE **PRICE** CHANGES

If aggregate demand increases, it shifts to the right (AKA **positive demand shock**)  
If aggregate demand decreases, it shifts to the left (AKA **negative demand shock**)

Aggregate demand shifters

- Expectations  
  - If consumers and firms become more optimistic →⬆️  
  - If consumers and firms become more  pessimistic→⬇️  
- Wealth  
  - If the real value of HH assets rises →⬆️  
  - If the real value of HH assets falls → ⬇️  
- Size of existing stock of physical capital  
  - If the existing stock of physical capital is relatively small →⬆️  
  - If the existing stock of physical capital is relatively large →⬇️  
- Fiscal policy  
  - If the government increases spending or cuts taxes →⬆️  
  - If the government decreases spending or increases taxes→⬇️  
- Monetary policy  
  - If the central bank increases the quantity of money→⬆️  
  - If the central bank reduces the quantity of money→⬇️  
- Net exports  
  - If there is an increase in spending on domestic g/s → ⬆️  
  - If there is a decrease in spending on domestic g/s →⬇️  
- Interest rates  
  - An event (besides a change in APL) causes lower interest rates →⬆️  
  - An event (besides a change in APL) causes higher interest rates →⬇️

Income \= Yd \+ taxes

3.3 Aggregate supply curves  
Short run \- when prices are not fully flexible

Recession/expansion indicators

- Aggregate output measured by real GDP  
- Price level stability is measured by the Aggregate Price level and the inflation rate  
- Unemployment rate 

**Short-run Aggregate Supply Curve (SRAS)**

- positive association between APL & Y

![][image17]  
**Profit per unit** \= price per unit \- production cost

**Production cost**, aka. **Input costs**

Do not account for inflation in price or nominal wages in the short run 

SRAS has a positive slope bc input prices are **sticky** (don’t change as much or as quickly as the APL)

![][image18]

**POVS:**  
Typically, sign a contract with companies for wages → negotiate wages upon renewal of contract → making people wait for contract makes the input price of nominal   
wages **sticky**

*Business owner/producer*

- Recession  
  - Wants to make a profit → look at ways to cut production costs/input prices → lower wages to keep as much profit as possible, as the economy is stagnating  
- Expansion  
  - increased profit → *Could* pay workers more bc they’re making more profit → want to keep good workers → will give workers higher wages that they demand to retain the workforce

*Employee/worker*

- Recession  
  - People losing jobs across the economy → willing to accept lower nominal wages in order to keep their jobs  
- Expansion  
  - Know that companies can pay them more → rising prices → demand higher wages → are paid more by their current job or go find another job bc jobs are available in expansion

![][image19]

⬆️⬇️

SRAS shifters

- Change in commodity prices  
  - If commodity prices fall → ⬆️  
  - If commodity prices rise →⬇️  
- Change in normal wages  
  - If nominal wages fall → ⬆️   
  - If nominal wages rise →⬇️  
- Change in productivity  
  - If workers become more productive → ⬆️  
  - If workers become less productive → ⬇️  
- Business taxes  
  - If the government cuts business taxes →⬆️  
  - If the government increases business taxes → ⬇️  
- *Expectation* about inflation \+ input prices  
  - If the producers expect inflation to be lower → ⬆️  
  - If the producers expect inflation to be higher →⬇️  
- Legal-institutional environment  
  - higher taxes or regulation → ⬇️  
  - Lower taxes, more subsidies, or less regulation → ⬆️

![][image20]

**Shifters of LRAS**

Right shift  →  economic growth 

- Productivity  
  - If there’s an increase in physical capital, human capital, or tech. → ⬆️  
  - If there’s an increase in physical capital, human capital, or tech. → ⬇️  
- Quantity of resources  
  - If there’s an increase in the quantity or resources → ⬆️  
  - If there’s an increase in the quantity or resources → ⬇️

**Potential output** \- the level of GDP the economy would produce if all prices were fully flexible

- Also would be at a point of full employment of resources (not meaning everyone is employed, just that we are at the **natural rate of unemployment (NRU)**)

**Non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU)**

Equilibrium (3-4)  
Output gap as percentage \= \[(Y-Yp)/Yp\] x 100

**Recessionary gap (Rg → not accepted by AP)** \- when output is lower than potential output (AKA recessionary gap)

- In recession

**Inflationary gap (Ig → not accepted abbrev. By AP)**\- when output is higher than potential output (AKA positive output gap)

- expansion

3.5 fiscal policy  
**Stabilization policies** \- when gov. Intervenes in economy 

- **Fiscal policy** \- conducted by executive & legislative branches  
- **Monetary policy** \- conducted by country’s central bank  
  - American central bank \= **Federal Reserve** (Fed)  
  - Central bank is part of gov., but is an independent regulatory organization meant to be impartial to politics

**Expansionary fiscal policy** to get out of **recession**

**Contractionary fiscal policy** to get out of **expansion**

**Aggregate discretion** \- Fiscal policy enacted through automatic stabilizer or discretionary spending

- Gov. has to change or do something to enact that policy

**Automatic stabilizers** automatically happen based on economy’s setup

Get back to equilibrium through shocks \- SRAS

fiscal policy gets back to equilibrium w/ AD

Measuring economic performance  
2-1 Business cycles and GDP

**Economic indicators:** 

- Inflation  
- Housing  
- GDP  
- War  
- Oil

3 primary indicators:

1. **Aggregate output** – total goods and services in the economy  
   1. Measured with GDP  
2. **Employment of resources**  
   1. Measured with the unemployment rate  
3. **Price level stability**

In an **expansion**: 

- GDP goes up (production up)  
- Unemployment rate down (use more workers to make more stuff)  
- APL/IR goes up (workers paid more, more money floating around economy

In a **recession** (TYPICALLY)

- GDP down (production down)  
- UR up  
- APL/IR down

Unique case: 70s → **Stagflation**

- GDP down  
- UR up  
- APL/IR up

**Depression** \- either a really long or a really bad recession

- Had such a bad experience in the Great Depression that people are scared of the term

If people think a depression or recession is coming, they can alter their behaviors and actually cause one

**National income accounts/accounting**

- Collect stats. On GDP to use in business cycle  
- Decide what data is included  
- Loans not included in GDP

3 approaches to calculating GDP

- **Value-added approach**  
  * Price x quantity (P \*Q)  of all final goods and services  
  * Subtract out input(21,500-9000) \+ (9000-4200) \+ 4200 \= \$21,500 (GDP)  
- **Expenditure approach**  
  * Calculate the spending of each sector of the economy (product market)  
    * Households (consumption \[C\]), firms (investment \[I\]), government (government spending \[G\]), world (Net Exports minus imports \[EX \- IM\])  
  * Nominal GDP adds up the spending of all sectors  
  * Doesn’t include underground market (drug dealers)  
- **Income approach**  
  * Track the income households are receiving in the factor market  
    * Land, labor, capital, entrepreneuriability  
    * GDP \= rent \+ wages \+ interest \+ profit

Output and Growth (2.2)  
Limitations of GDP

Statistical discrepancies

- Errors in collecting data & doing math  
- Missing out on the nuance of aggregating data  
- Not counting non-market data  
  * household production or underground (black market) activity  
- Doesn’t account for price changes  
  * GDP can rise because of increased production OR a price increase

Nominal vs. Real values

- **Nominal values** \- don’t account for inflation; don’t remove effects of inflation from real values  
- **Real values** \- account for inflation; remove effects of inflation from real values

GDP doesn’t tell us about product quality either

Find real GDP by comparing prices and quantities of different years relative to each other Calculate non-real GDP

Know the general process of income and expenditure approaches

**Standard of living**

- GDP only tells us a dollar value, not how stable a government is in a country, or about the quality of life  
- Try to get a better idea of the quality of living with GDP per capita  
  - GDP/population size \= GDP per capita  
  - Used to understand economic growth better

**Externalities** \- positive and negative effects of production

- Also not included in GDP

GDP gives indication of economic growth, but ONLY focuses on dollar amounts

Unemployment Rate  
Measuring employment of our resources/FoP

- Mostly focus on labor

Calculated by bureau of labor statistics (BLS)

1) Break down population (U.S. citizens) into 2 different groups: younger than 16 years old and 16+  
   1) Not really looking at people \>16  
2) Break 16+ into 3 groups:   
   1) Employed (working in any capacity with proper documentation)  
   2) Unemployed (people not working who are actively looking for work)  
   3) Not in labor force  
      1) Retired  
      2) Disability  
      3) Discouraged workers  
      4) Nepo babies  
      5) Students who aren’t working  
      6) Incarcerated  
      7) Household production (stay at home, etc.)

Employed \+ Unemployed \= Labor force (LF)

Labor force participation rate (LFPR) equation:  
LFPR % \= 100(LF/Population 16+)  
Unemployment Rate equation:   
UR% \= 100(\#Unemployed/LF)

Different types of unemployment:

- Frictional (part of natural rate of unemployment)  
- Structural (also part of NRU)  
- cyclical unemployment

NRU can change because of makeup of labor force, changes in labor institutions, and changes in government policies

- Ex.: retirement of baby boomers, tech., entry of women into the labor force, unions, etc.   
- NRU will often equal point where we have full employment of resources (not 100%, but close enough) and a point where we have potential output (Yₚ)

Limitations:

- Statistical discrepancies  
  - Errors in collecting data, errors in doing math  
- Doesn’t account for variation among groups  
- Doesn’t capture marginally attached workers  
- Doesn’t capture underemployed

Price level stability (2-4)  
APL → **aggregate price level**

Price level doesn’t matter as much as **purchasing power**  
   
**Transaction costs**

- **Shoeleather** \- when inflation causes transaction costs to rise  
- **Menu** \- printing  
- **Unit of account** \-  made difficult to compare prices and make economic calculations

Nominal vs. Real prices

**Effects of inflation**  
Who is hurt by unexpected inflation?

- People on a fixed income  
- Savers/lenders

Unaffected/helped?

- Flexible income/borrowers

Inflation rate calculated by **Beureau of labor statistics**

1) Calculate **market basket**   
   1) Look at quantity of items people are buying and the prices that those items cost → always look at at least two years, both prices and quantities can change from year to year  
   2) (P x Q) \+ (P x Q) \+ (P x Q)...  
   3) Ex.: limes, bananas, and peppers  
      1) 2020: (\$.40 x 200 limes) \+ (\$.60 x 50 bananas) \+ (\$.25 x 100 peppers) \= \$95  
      2) 2021: (\$.40 x 200 limes) \+ (\$1 x 50 bananas) \+ (\$.45 x 100 peppers) \= \$175  
2) Construct a **price index**  
   1) Normalize data \- show number in terms of 100 in base year  
      1) Base year either told to us in directions or is the earliest time period  
   2) CPI \= consumer price index  
      1) Look at consumer price index for households of four  
      2) CPI(given) \= \[MB(given)/MB(base)\] x 100  
         1) given=CPI in year we’re looking for  
      3) CPI\*2020 \= \[\$95/\$95\] x 100 \= 100  
      4) CPI \* 2021 \= \[\$175/\$95\] x 100 \= 184.2  
3) Calculate **inflation rate**  
   1) IR% \= \[(CPInew \- CPIold)/CPIold\] x 100  
      1) IR% \= \[(184.2 \- 100\) / 100\] x 100 \= 84.2%

Limitations to inflation rate:

1) Statistical discrepancies (errors in collecting data and doing math)  
2) Missing out on groups (urban and rural populations, families of more or less than 4\)  
3) Doesn’t account for **substitution bias**  
   1) Doesn’t take into account substituting one item for another  
4) Doesn’t account for trickflation or shrinkflation

BLS calculates inflation rate in two ways to account for statistical discrepancies

- GDP deflator \= \[Nominal GDP / Y\] x 100

| **GDP** | Total value of all final goods and services produced in a country’s borders in a given period of time | Value in dollars; only looking at value of all FINAL g/s Not talking about inputs |
| **Economic indicator** | Tells us where we are in the economy |  |
| **consumption** | Households buying & consuming goods | Doesn’t include buying used products or household production |
| **investment** | Spending of firms; investments in physical or human capital; includes both planned and unplanned investments | DOES NOT INCLUDE INPUTS Unplanned investments → replace broken things Investment includes inventories |
| **Government spending** | Spending by the government on goods and services | Building roads, buying a tank, paying public school teachers; doesn’t include transfer payments |
| **Transfer payment** | Any time money exchanges hands without a good, service, resource, or asset being provided in return | Happens publicly (involving gov.) and privately (not involving gov.) Ex.: gifts (priv.), medicare, stimulus checks, medicaid, unemployment support (public) |
| **Net exports** |  |  |
| **Nominal values** |  don’t account for inflation; don’t remove effects of inflation from real values |  |
| **Real values** | account for inflation; remove effects of inflation from real values |  |
| **chainlinking** | Look at the prices of one year and the quantity of another |  |
| **Esternalities** | Positive and negative effects of production |  |
| **Frictional Unemployment** | Arises from normal labor turnover; includes duration of job search; momentary unemployment | Decide to quit job, looking for another job, haven’t quite found one yet |
| **Structural unemployment** | When \# of people searching for jobs in labor market \> \# jobs available; typically due to technological advances | Ex.: telephone operators |
| **Cyclical unemployment** | Arises from where we are in the business cycle; when we enter into a recession, the unemployment we get as result of a recession |  |
| **Marginally attached workers** | People who don’t have a job but would like a job, but they’ve given up looking; feel like they’re unemployed |  |
| **Discouraged workers** | Type of marginally attached workers; gave up looking for work due to the state of the job market |  |
| **underemployed** | Have jobs, but are not working as many hours as they would like and/or are not fully using their human capital as they’d like to |  |
| **Purchasing power** | Our ability to pay prices |  |
| **Inflation (rate)** | General increase in prices; how quickly the prices are rising |  |
| **deflation** | General decrease in prices; how quickly the prices are decreasing | If prices go down for long period of time → either have to accept lower wages or lose your job |
| **disinflation** | Still inflation; prices going up at decreasing rate | If they were going up fast before, now theyre still going up but slower |
| **hyperinflation** | Inflation at an ever increasing rate |  |
| **Shoeleather costs** | When inflation causes transaction costs to rise |  |
| **transaction** | Additional time, energy, and effort that it takes to do something |  |
| **Menu costs** | Cost of printing prices | Ex.: digital signs for gas prices because the price always changes, so they can’t keep reprinting it |
| **Unit of account** | Our ability to compare prices and make economic calculations | Ex.: getting house price evaluated from year to year changes not bc. Of anything physical, but because of inflation or deflation |
| **shrinkflation** | Rather than increase in price for consumers, decrease amount in products | Ex.: fewer doritos in each dorito bag sold → because of production costs or company just trying to make more money? |

1.1  
Economics \- study of scarcity and choice  
**Economics** \- the study of how people fulfill their unlimited wants and needs in a world where resources are scarce

**Resources** are **scarce**

- **Trade-offs**  
  - Limited income and time are barriers to people having everything that they want  
    - Willing to trade money for time (ex.: convinience stores charge higher price than large supermarkets → travel less time, but pay more)  
  - Individuals have to make choices because resources are scarce  
- **Resources**  
  - Resource is scarce when there is not enough to satisfy ways society wants to use it  
  - Factors of production  
  - Inputs used to produce a good (g) or service (s) that people want  
-   
  - 4 categories: land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship  
    - **land** : all natural resources used to produce g/s  
      - *the payoff for land is rent*  
    - **labor** : the physical or mental effort used to produce g/s  
      - *Payoff for labor is wages*  
    - **Capital** : aides or tools used to produce g/s  
      - *Payoff for capital is interest*  
      - 2 types:  
        - **Physical capital** (buildings, tools, machines, equipment, workspace)  
        - **Human capital**: acquired knowledge & skill  
    - **Entrepreneurial ability** \-    
      - *Payoff for Entreprenurial ability is profit*

**Scarcity** vs. **shortage** → scarcity is when we will never be able to fulfill demand, shortage is when there isn’t enough supply for a limited amount of time

- Society vs. individual choices  
  - Society can make choices by allowing them to emerge out of many individual choices   
    - Ex.: Americans must decide how to spend their time → society’s choice about where to shop is the sum of Americans’ choices 

**Opportunity Cost**: The Real Cost of Something is What You Must Give Up to Get It

- Opportunity cost  
  - The cost of other, forgone options when you make a decision  
  - All costs are opportunity costs

**Social sciences**

- Use scientific methods to study how people interact with each other and the world  
  - Economic model: small, simplified version of real world

**Assumption**

- People have unlimited wants but limited resources, so they **must make choices**  
- Because of scarcity, we assume that **nothing is free** (no such thing as free lunch)  
- Rational pursuit of self interest: assume that individuals look for or pursue opportunities to increase their utility

Rational pursuit of self interest comes from **marginal analysis**

- Involves considering **incentives**, **trade-offs**, **transaction costs**, & **opportunity costs**

Sometimes will see opportunity costs as \$0 → just means that monetary cost is not the incentive

- opportunity cost is the opportunity lost

The **invisible hand theory**

- Adam Smith  
  - Coined both invisible hand theory and capitalism  
- If everyone is acting the rational pursuit of self interest, society as a whole benefits as if an invisible hand is guiding each individual  
- Market failure – when invisible hand doesn’t work

What are we going to produce given our resources?

For whom are we going to produce these things?

Know Broad social goals & types of economies

Sectors:  
Individuals → Households → firms → government (all levels) → rest of world (all economies)

**Households** supply things (labor, capital, etc.) → all other sectors demand it

Sectors interact with each other in **markets**

- Factor/resource market  
- Product market  
- Financial market

1.3 \-   
1.4 \- Advantage and Trade  
20 peaches & zero fish or 10 fish & zero peaches

- Opportunity cost of fish is 20 peaches (-2)  
- Opportunity cost of 20 peaches is 10 fish (-0.5)

Absolute advantage & specialization

Law of Comparative advantage

Terms of trade need to be rooted in opportunity cost  
(allison won’t pay more than 2 peaches to get a fish, bc she could just get it on her own)  
Consumers & demand  
In a competitive market, there are buyers and sellers 

- None can control price or prevent others from entering or exiting the market

If demand increases, quantity demanded increases and the curve shifts to the right

If demand decreases, curve shifts to the left and 

Market size (Boomer gen.)  
Tastes & preferences (beanie Babies, Labubus)  
Income of consumers (ramen v. name brand pasta)  
Consumer expectations (gas on labor day)

- When expect price to go up, demand go up

**Percent change \= \[new/old\] x 100**  
If the percent change is less than 1, it's **inelastic**; exactly one \= **unit elastic**; **elastic** \= greater than one

**Diminishing marginal utility** → enjoyment/utility of something diminishes over time

Producers & supply  
When P goes up, QS goes up                         when P goes down, QS goes down

When supply increases, curve shifts to right

- Comes with better tech. 

When supply decreases, curve shifts to left 

- Can look like increasing, but all QS is lower  
- Can be bc of extreme weather 

![][image23]  
Market Equilibrium   
price is really high → demand low

Demand \= entire relationship  
Specific quantity \= quantity demanded  
Price never \= 0

![][image24]  
In this scenario, there is a shortage of apples → price start going up & quantity production increased  
![][image25]

Raise price to \$3, quantity supplied also 3000lbs → quantity demanded low b/c price is higher → now have a surplus in quantity of apples produced ![][image26]

reduce price to sell extra apples & produce fewer apples, increasing demand again  
![][image27]  
All go toward the point of intersection between price and quantity where the price is where quantity supplied is equal to the quantity demanded called the **equilibrium price** (\$2.15/2200lbs. In this case)

Changes in equilibrium price and quantity  
If new disease resistant apple invented → allow producers to produce more apples, shifting the quantity supplied up at any given price point

- supply curve shift to right  
- minimum price to produce apples is lower

Pink circles on price axis \= new and old equilibrium prices

If study finds that apples prevent cancer, demand goes up 

- Price will go up  
- Demand curve will shift right  
- Quantity also goes up  
- More people want apples than cancer

Pear cider industry launches ad campaign  
(assume same people growing apples grow pears)

- Demand rises for cider relative to apple cider  
  * Apple demand will go down  
  * Entire demand curve shift to left  
  * Quantity produced for pears rises  
  * Supply of apples goes down  
- Substitutes  
- Equilibrium price is constant while equilibrium quantity changed  
- Supply of apples drop much more than demand did, so price went up

Apple pickers demand wage increases

- Cost of production goes up → less willing to produce apples  
  * At given price pt., lower quantity supplied  
  * Lower supply → higher price

**Price Controls**  
Price ceiling \- the cap on a price that the government sets so the price can’t go to equilibrium

- Problem: @ lower price, consumers want to buy more while producers want to produce less, creating a shortage

Price floor \- minimum price that buyers are expected to pay for a product

- When price goes up, QS goes up → doesn’t really help because then consumers don’t want to buy more expensive corn  
  - Lead to surplus

Floor must be above equilibrium  
Ceiling goes below equilibrium  
(flipped house)

 Demand (D) Quantity of goods consumers are willing to purchase at various prices

Quantity demanded (QD) \- quantity consumers are willing and able to purchase at a specific price

| Term | Definition | Significance/examples |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Demand** | Quantity of goods consumers are willing to purchase at various prices | Whole curve on demand schedule |
| **Quantity Demanded** | Quantity consumers are willing and able to purchase at a specific price | A specific point on demand schedule |
| **Demand schedule** | Quantity and demand data in a table graph | Price on Y axis, demand on X axis; negative slope; whole curve is demand, a specific point on curve is quantity demanded |
| **Substitution effect** | When price changes, consumers led to change behavior and substitute one item for another | Get coffee every day for \$3. Next day, coffee is \$10 a cup. Because of price raise, switch to tea |
| **Income effect** | When price changes make consumers feel like they have a different amount of money, which makes them change their spending behavior |  |
| **Law of Demand** | When price increases, quantity demanded decreases |  |
| **Normal goods** | Everyday products |  |
| **Inferior goods** | Secondhand, store brand, generic | Not many people buy when have high income |
| **Substitute in consumption** | one or more goods and services where consumers buy one or the other | Pepsi and coke, powerade and gatorade |
| **Complements of consumption** | Two or more items that consumers buy together | Bacon and eggs, peanut butter and jelly \- market/demand for one impacts market/demand for other |
| **elasticity** | A consumer’s responsiveness to a price change | Most products are elastic |

**Crash Courses 10/13**  
*Why are competitive markets proven to be more successful at providing what people want?*

Central planned economy → everyone who wants a job has a job.\], but reality is less ideal for consumers → inefficient

- Central planners not as focused on production cost, while free-market gives business owners an incentive (profit) not to be wasteful (**production efficiency**)  
- Ex.: Russia focused on producing tractors and military vehicles \> soap, coffee, smartphones  
- (**Allocative efficency**) central planners less likely to be allocatively efficient because they can’t get feedback about product demand, while free market producers learn about demand through market research and looking at prices

Competition between businesses keeps prices and quality up (Invisible Hand Theory \- *Adam Smith)* 

The United States is not a free market economy → everything is regulated (FDA, controlled market for National Defense, etc.)

Price gouging exploits consumers → anti-price gouging laws exist in several states in the U.S. 

- Do they make the problem worse? → allowing prices to increase in times of crisis encourages others outside the disaster zone to haul in and sell essential goods  
- If prices can’t increse, there’s less of an incentive to bring things in

Desire to earn profit keeps prices down

Businesses can get more business by responding well in times of crisis (PR)

Predatory pricing lawsuits are common, but rarely successful

Capitalism, with its system of price signals, is basically crowdfunding

- Collectively choose what we want and what is made  
- Ex.: Starbucks and Target boycotts

Monopolies and Anti-competitive markets

In most cases, we want to prevent monopolies, not celebrate them

- Monopolies keep competitors out of the market with **barriers to entry**  
- Profit increase by eliminating competition → move all demand to one spot in market

Companies don’t need a literal monopoly to exercise monopoly power

- Single company (like google or microsoft) holds a huge market share, it can exercise its power in a similar way to a monopoly

Most economists support antitrust laws (Teddy Roosevelt and W.H. Taft v. Rockefeller, Carnegie, Vanderbilt, etc.)

- **Sherman Act** \- “if we will not endure a king as a political power, we should not endure a king over the production, transportation, and sale of any of the necessities of life” (John Sherman, 3:58)  
  - Outlaws monopolization or attempted monopolization  
  - Mergers need to be government approved to prevent monopolies → coke couldn’t buy pepsi

Anti-trust regulations can also prevent companies from making anti-competitive deals with their suppliers

- Microsoft suit → accused of pressuring PC sellers to integrate Internet Explorer to exclude Netscape, their main competitor


Patent guarantees right to be a monopoly for amount of time (typically 20 years) 

- Encourage innovation → make profit on product, then eventually competition can move in and lower prices

Monopolies can charge more for products than they could if they had competitors

Game Theory and Oligopoly  
“Oligopolies often sell products that are similar but not identical” (2:05), giving them some control over their prices

- → **non-price competition** (advertising)  
  - “Half the money spent on advertising is wasted; the trouble is, you don’t know which half” \- Don Draper  
- Monopolies and perfect competitive markets don’t run ads because they don’t need to; they either own the whole market or produce identical goods, so ads just increase their costs and drives up their prices

GAME THEORY

- Prisoner’s dilemma  
- Even if people and companies rationally follow their own self-interest, the best outcome is hard to reach when they can’t or don’t cooperate

Payoff matrix  
![][image29]

- Explains why collusion and cartels are unstable   
- Best outcome for stan \= Stan’s best response (pricing low if Brandon prices high)  
- Pricing low always results in a better outcome

“At its best, healthy competition promotes innovation, which, in the end, makes us all better off” (9:15)

| Term | Definition | Significance/examples |

| **Sole Proprietorship** | A business firm owned by one person | Advantages: Easiest \+ inexpensive to set up, ease of decision-making, tax benefits, owner keeps profits, can be your own boss  Disadvantages: the owner is responsible for everything, funding problems, and unlimited liability |
| **Partnership** | A business with two or more owners | Advantages: more financing, shared decision-making Disadvantages: unlimited liability, partners may disagree |
| **Coroporation** | A business firm that is itself a legal entity owned by stockholders | Advantages: Limited liability for stockholders, easy fundraising through stocks or bonds, rapid growth Disadvantages: expensive start-up costs, delays in decision-making, low or non-monetary rewards, divided profits, double taxation, and more regulations |
| **Limited liability corporation** | A hybrid business organization that combines features of corporations, partnerships, and sole proprietorships | Advantages: easy to form, can avoid double taxation of profit, personal assets are protected from creditors Disadvantages: can’t raise funds by selling shares of stock |
| **Franchise** | A parent company and numerous associated businesses that sell a standardized good or service | Advantages: proven product and good reputation Disadvantages: ongoing and startup fees might be high, the franchisor maintains some control over products and prices |
| **Cooperative** | A business owned by its members and operated to supply members and others with goods and services | Advantages: members supply labor, assets are distributed to members after expenses are paid, gain purchasing power Disadvantages: members may shirk responsibility and cannot change the prices |
| **Non-profit corporation** | A legal entity formed to carry out a “not-for-profit” mission | Advantages: don’t pay taxes, are eligible for grants or other government aid, high social satisfaction Disadvantages: don’t earn profits, rely on volunteers to perform much of the work, strict reporting requirements, getting grants and paperwork can be tedious |

| **patent** | Grants inventor exclusive rights to profit from a specific product or process | Encourage innovation |

## **The Island of Econia**

Once upon a time, two friends—**Lena** and **Kai**—were stranded on a deserted island called **Econia**. They needed two things to survive: **fish** and **coconuts**.

Lena could catch **10 fish** or collect **20 coconuts** in a day.

Kai could catch **5 fish** or collect **15 coconuts** in a day.

---

### **Opportunity Cost**

Every day, they had to decide how to spend their time. If Lena spent her day catching fish, she gave up the chance to gather coconuts—and vice versa. Her **opportunity cost** of catching 1 fish was **2 coconuts** (20 coconuts ÷ 10 fish).

For Kai, the **opportunity cost** of catching 1 fish was **3 coconuts** (15 ÷ 5).

---

### **Absolute Advantage**

Lena was better than Kai at **everything**. She could catch more fish and collect more coconuts in the same amount of time. Economists say Lena had an **absolute advantage** in both tasks.

But being better at everything doesn’t mean she should do everything.

---

### **Comparative Advantage & Specialization**

Though Lena had an absolute advantage in both fish and coconuts, she had a **lower opportunity cost** for catching fish (2 coconuts per fish), while Kai had a lower opportunity cost for collecting coconuts (he only gave up 1.67 fish per 5 coconuts, or 1 fish per 3 coconuts).

So, Lena had a **comparative advantage** in fishing, and Kai had a **comparative advantage** in collecting coconuts.

They decided to **specialize**:

* Lena spent all day catching fish.

* Kai spent all day collecting coconuts.

---

### **Gains from Trade**

After one day:

* Lena caught **10 fish**.

* Kai collected **15 coconuts**.

They agreed to trade: Lena gave Kai **4 fish** in exchange for **8 coconuts**.

Now they each had:

* Lena: **6 fish** \+ **8 coconuts**

* Kai: **4 fish** \+ **7 coconuts**

Compare this to what they could produce **individually** in a mixed day (e.g., if Lena split her time, she'd get 5 fish and 10 coconuts; Kai would get 2.5 fish and 7.5 coconuts). They were both **better off** by specializing and trading.

This is called the **gains from trade**.

---

## **Moral of the Story**

Even if one person is better at everything (absolute advantage), it can still benefit both people to specialize in what they’re **relatively** better at (comparative advantage) and **trade**—leading to more total resources and a better standard of living.
